title: Your bio and your filter
header_line: Jose's analysis of a book we are still naming. Not a summary of the book. Not affiliated with or endorsed by the author or publisher.

lines.text: Does your bio make the wrong people say no?

groups.heading: A bio in the third person

lines.text: Jose said that he took a student's bio, edited it and wrote an example to show how. He said to write it in the third person, as if you were someone else, and not to pull punches.
A student said that the opening paragraphs were better than their own.

Jose said that one sentence is where you start to filter people: your successes come from working with clients clearly focused on a certain result. You can be successful or unsuccessful with someone, and this tells them if they fit.
He said you can politely say: you do not fit the profile of the clients I am successful with, and I cannot really help you at this stage.
Jose said you need one sentence describing what you do, the elevator sentence, and you can say it at a cocktail party or a restaurant when you bump into somebody.
He said he went broad, then specific, then specific, and closed into something very specific with a lot of power, and then added leadership to show you are not only an individual.

exercise.title: Five minutes
steps: Write your bio in the third person in five lines.
Write the sentence that filters out the wrong clients.
Write who you want to close in on, specifically.
Write one line that shows your leadership.

check.q: What did Jose say to write your bio in?
What does the filter sentence do?

choices: One sentence on what you do

recap: Write your bio in the third person. Filter with one sentence.
